cues.text: A Grief the Ancient World Understood Well
Neither Joachim nor Anne is named anywhere in the canonical Gospels.

Everything the Church has treasured about them across the centuries comes instead from early Christian tradition, chiefly a text known as the Protoevangelium of James , dating to the mid-second century.
It is a source outside the inspired Scriptures that preserves early Christian traditions about them, though its historical details cannot be verified in every particular.
That tradition tells us Joachim and Anne were a devout, married couple advanced in years.
In a culture that regarded bearing children as an essential mark of divine favor, their childlessness brought personal sorrow and public shame.

Joachim reportedly turned away on one occasion from presenting his offering in the Temple because Reuben told him it was not fitting for a man without offspring to be first among those offering sacrifice.
Into the Wilderness to Pray
Grieved by this rejection, Joachim withdrew into the wilderness, fasting for forty days and nights, unwilling to return home until God had answered his petition.
Anne, meanwhile, learning the reason for her husband's prolonged and unexplained absence, poured out her anguish to God in solitude beneath a laurel tree in her garden.
She wept over her double sorrow — the loneliness of having a husband absent, and childlessness besides.
She promised that if her prayer for a child were answered, she would dedicate that child entirely to God's service, in an echo of the ancient prayer of Hannah for the prophet Samuel.
A Prayer Answered by Angels
Tradition holds that an angel appeared to each of them in turn: Joachim in the wilderness and Anne beneath her laurel tree.
The angel promised that their long years of barren waiting were about to end, and that the child born to them would be spoken of throughout the whole world.
Joachim, filled with joy, hurried home to his wife.
The two, tradition tells us, met and embraced at the city gate—a reunion later Christian art would render again and again as a tender image of hope restored after long sorrow.

Whatever we make of the precise historical details of this account, it points toward a truth the Church has always confessed: the coming of Mary , and through her of Christ himself, was prepared quietly and patiently.
It unfolded across generations of ordinary faithful longing, not in some single dramatic instant divorced from the slow, human texture of prayer and waiting.
Grandparents of the Redeemer
The daughter born to Joachim and Anne, tradition holds, was named Miriam — Mary — and was raised by her parents in devout expectation of God's promises to Israel.
Some traditions even hold that she was presented, as a small child of only three years old, for a period of formation within the precincts of the Jerusalem Temple.
This fulfilled the very vow her mother had made in her own hour of grief.
Whatever the precise historical shape of Mary's own upbringing, the Church has always recognized something profoundly significant in Joachim and Anne.

They were the grandparents of the Redeemer, whose patient, faithful longing for a child became, without their knowing it then, the first faithful link in the chain leading directly to the Incarnation of the Son of God.
Patrons of Every Long Waiting
Devotion to Sts. Joachim and Anne spread gradually from the Christian East, where their story had long been treasured, into the Western Church.
Their devotion gained particular strength from the thirteenth century onward.
Today their images — Anne especially, often shown teaching the young Mary to read Scripture, a tender and instructive detail of later Christian art — remain beloved throughout the Catholic world.
Couples who have endured years of longing for a child, grandparents handing on the faith, and anyone who has prayed for years without visible answer have long found companions in Joachim and Anne.
They understand that particular, patient form of hope—a hope that does not grow bitter with delay but continues, year after year, to trust.
Shrines of Enduring Devotion
Two shrines above all carry their memory forward into the present day: Sainte-Anne-d'Auray in Brittany, France, and Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré in Quebec, Canada.
Both are important pilgrimage sites in their respective countries, attracting countless pilgrims over many generations.
These pilgrims bring to St. Anne, in particular, their own prayers for children, family healing, and the grace of a patient, persevering faith.
Legacy
Though the New Testament itself is silent about them, the Church's ancient veneration of Joachim and Anne reflects a truth worth holding onto in every generation.
The great events of salvation history are almost always prepared for in silence, by the faithful, largely unrecorded lives of ordinary believers—grandparents, in this case.
Their own years of prayer and patient waiting became, in God's providence, the hidden root from which the whole flowering of the Gospel would eventually grow.
